headline: High risk of prompt injection and cascading errors: Cursor can ingest shared files/clipboard and run tools, while mem0 can be fed unverified outputs as memory.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor reads workspace files, open buffers, clipboard, and uses MCP; mem0 is a memory layer that can receive agent outputs. A shared local filesystem and clipboard create a plausible injection bridge, though not a guaranteed one. The pathway is stronger than low because Cursor may treat file content as trusted, but weaker than high because no documented raw-web parsing or shared MCP provenance gap is shown for mem0.
conditions: IF mem0 ingests Cursor-produced text into persistent memory without sanitization
IF Cursor opens or summarizes attacker-controlled workspace files or clipboard content as instructions
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between the tools
Use a dedicated, isolated workspace directory
Require explicit provenance tags on any text passed from Cursor to mem0
Turn off MCP servers unless needed
Review any imported memory entries before persistence

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, clipboard contents, and has broad network egress; mem0 is a knowledge-management system that may store or retrieve those outputs. The pair can therefore move sensitive workspace data into a second system by default if the operator connects them, creating a realistic leakage path. I cite both agents because the risk depends on Cursor's data access and mem0's memory role.
conditions: IF Cursor forwards open-file or clipboard content into mem0 memory entries
IF the shared workspace contains secrets or proprietary source code
mitigations: Exclude secrets files from Cursor's workspace
Redact clipboard content before any transfer
Store only summaries in mem0, not raw text
Use separate accounts or tenants for the two tools
Audit recent memory writes for sensitive strings

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; its concurrency model shares state via the local filesystem. mem0 is not shown to have locking or coordination primitives, so overlapping writes to shared mutable resources can race or corrupt state. This is high because default Cursor behavior already includes dangerous write paths and git mutation, while mem0's coordination is undocumented, so uncertainty escalates.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or memory-backed store
IF Cursor runs in Yolo mode or otherwise auto-executes file-changing commands
mitigations: Assign separate directories for each agent
Disable Yolo mode for shared repos
Add file locks around shared mutable paths
Pause mem0 writes during Cursor git operations
Use a single orchestrator to serialize writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor's agent loop can generate code, facts, or summaries that mem0 may later store and reuse as authoritative memory. If mem0 re-injects those entries into later prompts without verification, an initial mistake can cascade across sessions. The pathway is plausible in default integrations, but mem0 is not shown to take external actions itself, so high is not justified.
conditions: IF mem0 stores Cursor-generated claims without source attribution
IF later prompts retrieve those claims as trusted context
mitigations: Require citations for any stored memory item
Mark machine-generated memories as untrusted
Add a human review step before persistence
Limit retrieval to high-confidence memories only
Expire low-confidence memories quickly

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor explicitly handles model-provider API keys and open files, while mem0's profile does not show regulated-data certifications or residency constraints. The only concrete compliance concern visible is that Cursor may process sensitive workspace data, but there is no documented mismatch such as HIPAA or EU residency conflict for mem0. I do not cite mem0-specific compliance fields because none are present.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is placed into Cursor-managed files
IF mem0 is configured to retain that data beyond the operator's policy
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Use synthetic or redacted examples
Set short retention on mem0 memories
Document a data-handling policy for both tools
Review exports and deletion behavior before use
